title: Matter Cycles and Earth's Spheres
seo_title: Grade 9 Science: Matter Cycles and Earth's Spheres Worksheets (BC Curriculum)
standard_text: The biosphere, geosphere, hydrosphere and atmosphere are interconnected, as matter cycles and energy flows through them: the carbon, water and nitrogen cycles, photosynthesis and cellular respiration, and energy flow in ecosystems. (summary of BC's Curriculum, Science 9, Earth and Space Science)
meta_desc: Free Grade 9 science worksheets (BC): Earth's four spheres, energy flow and food webs, the carbon and water cycles, photosynthesis and respiration. 100 questions with answers.
body_html:
How to think about it

Earth has four spheres: the biosphere (living things), geosphere (rock and soil), hydrosphere (water) and atmosphere (air). Matter such as carbon, water and nitrogen cycles between them and is reused.

Energy enters ecosystems as sunlight and flows from producers to consumers; about 90% is lost as heat at each step. Photosynthesis takes carbon dioxide from the air, and cellular respiration, decomposition and burning return it.

Example

Which process takes carbon dioxide out of the air?

Plants do it in sunlight.

Answer: photosynthesis

Example

Why does energy not cycle like matter?

Where does it go at each step?

Answer: it is lost as heat

Common mistakes

  • Saying energy cycles (matter cycles; energy flows).
  • Thinking plants get their mass from the soil.
  • Forgetting that decomposers return nutrients.

faq.q: Which sphere is a river in?
How does the ocean store carbon?
faq.a: It dissolves carbon dioxide, and sea creatures build shells from carbon.

items.q: More CO₂ helps some plants grow faster, and they take more CO₂ out of the air. What kind of feedback is this?
c: a feedback that only affects rocks
items.e: Positive feedback makes the change bigger; negative feedback makes it smaller.

items.q: Warmer air holds more water vapour, a greenhouse gas, which causes more warming. What kind of feedback is this?
c: a feedback that only affects rocks
items.e: Positive feedback makes the change bigger; negative feedback makes it smaller.

items.q: What is a flux in an Earth system model?
c: the rate at which matter or energy moves between reservoirs
items.e: Evaporation is a flux from ocean to atmosphere.

items.q: Warming melts sea ice, exposing dark ocean that absorbs more sunlight, which causes more warming. What kind of feedback is this?
c: a feedback that only affects rocks
items.e: Positive feedback makes the change bigger; negative feedback makes it smaller.

items.q: A dam is built across a river. Which other Earth system is most directly changed, and how?
c: the hydrosphere and biosphere (a lake forms, fish migration is blocked, sediment is trapped)
the atmosphere (cooler temperatures for a year or two)
items.e: A change in one sphere spreads to others.

items.q: What is a negative feedback loop?
c: a change that triggers effects that reduce the original change
a feedback that always warms Earth
a change that is made larger by its effects
items.e: Negative feedback tends to stabilize a system.

items.q: More CO₂ makes some plants grow faster and take up more CO₂. What kind of feedback is this?
items.e: It partly offsets the rise in CO₂.

items.q: More rainfall speeds up rock weathering, which removes CO₂ from the air over long times. What kind of feedback is this?
c: a feedback that only affects rocks
items.e: Positive feedback makes the change bigger; negative feedback makes it smaller.

items.q: Glaciers melt quickly in a warm period. Which other Earth system is most directly changed, and how?
c: the atmosphere (cooler temperatures for a year or two)
the hydrosphere and biosphere (a lake forms, fish migration is blocked, sediment is trapped)
items.e: A change in one sphere spreads to others.

items.q: Which sphere includes all of Earth's water, including ice and groundwater?
items.e: Ice is sometimes called the cryosphere.

items.q: Why do scientists use models of Earth systems?
c: to simplify complex systems so they can be explained and predictions tested
because models are always exactly right
items.e: All models have limitations.

items.q: Warmer oceans evaporate more water, forming more low clouds that reflect sunlight and cool the surface. What kind of feedback is this?
c: a feedback that only affects rocks
items.e: Positive feedback makes the change bigger; negative feedback makes it smaller.

items.q: Which four spheres make up the Earth system model?
c: crust, mantle, outer core and inner core
items.e: Matter and energy move between the spheres.

items.q: A large forest is cut down. Which other Earth system is most directly changed, and how?
c: the atmosphere and geosphere (more CO₂, more soil erosion)
the geosphere and hydrosphere (coasts erode faster without reefs)
the hydrosphere and biosphere (a lake forms, fish migration is blocked, sediment is trapped)
items.e: A change in one sphere spreads to others.

items.q: Warming thaws permafrost, which releases methane, which causes more warming. What kind of feedback is this?
c: a feedback that only affects rocks
items.e: Positive feedback makes the change bigger; negative feedback makes it smaller.

items.q: Drought kills plants, so less water evaporates from leaves, so less rain falls, making the drought worse. What kind of feedback is this?
c: a feedback that only affects rocks
items.e: Positive feedback makes the change bigger; negative feedback makes it smaller.

items.q: A volcano erupts and puts ash and gases high into the sky. Which other Earth system is most directly changed, and how?
c: the atmosphere and geosphere (more CO₂, more soil erosion)
the hydrosphere and biosphere (a lake forms, fish migration is blocked, sediment is trapped)
the atmosphere (cooler temperatures for a year or two)
items.e: A change in one sphere spreads to others.

items.q: What is a limitation of a box-and-arrow model of the water cycle?
c: it simplifies the system and may leave out how fluxes change over time and place
items.e: Models must be judged by how well they explain data.

items.q: A volcano releases sulfur dioxide that cools the climate. Which spheres interact?
c: the biosphere and the hydrosphere only
items.e: Volcanic gases enter the atmosphere.

items.q: Which sphere does the ozone layer belong to?
items.e: It is in the stratosphere.

items.q: Ethan's energy pyramid shows 50000 units of energy in the producers. About 10% passes to each level above. About how much energy reaches the primary consumers?
items.e: Divide by 10 for each level: 50000 → 5000.

items.q: The phytoplankton capture 5000 kJ of energy. Using the 10% rule, about how much reaches the small fish?
items.e: Divide by 10 for each step: 2 steps.

items.q: Why are there few snakes compared with grass?
c: Little energy reaches the top of the pyramid.
items.e: Less energy supports fewer animals.

items.q: Sofia's energy pyramid shows 20000 units of energy in the producers. About 10% passes to each level above. About how much energy reaches the secondary consumers?
items.e: Divide by 10 for each level: 20000 → 2000 → 200.

items.q: Why are there few tuna compared with phytoplankton?
c: Little energy reaches the top of the pyramid.
items.e: Less energy supports fewer animals.

items.q: What percent of the energy at one level passes to the next level?
Food chain: oak leaves → caterpillars → songbirds → foxes. What trophic level are the foxes?
items.e: Count from the producer.

items.q: The phytoplankton capture 2000 kJ of energy. Using the 10% rule, about how much reaches the tuna?
items.e: Divide by 10 for each step: 3 steps.

items.q: Use the 10% rule. How much energy reaches the grasshoppers?
Food chain: phytoplankton → zooplankton → small fish → tuna. What trophic level are the phytoplankton?
items.e: Count from the producer.

items.q: Food chain: phytoplankton → zooplankton → small fish → tuna. What trophic level are the tuna?
items.e: Count from the producer.

items.q: Leah's energy pyramid shows 20000 units of energy in the producers. About 10% passes to each level above. About how much energy reaches the tertiary consumers?
items.e: Divide by 10 for each level: 20000 → 2000 → 200 → 20.

items.q: The grass capture 2000 kJ of energy. Using the 10% rule, about how much reaches the snakes?
items.e: Divide by 10 for each step: 3 steps.

items.q: Kai's energy pyramid shows 2000 units of energy in the producers. About 10% passes to each level above. About how much energy reaches the tertiary consumers?
items.e: Divide by 10 for each level: 2000 → 200 → 20 → 2.

items.q: Food chain: algae → snails → crayfish → raccoons. What trophic level are the algae?
items.e: Count from the producer.

items.q: The algae capture 5000 kJ of energy. Using the 10% rule, about how much reaches the crayfish?
items.e: Divide by 10 for each step: 2 steps.

items.q: Where does most of the energy at each level go?
c: It stays stored forever in the top level.
It is recycled back to the producers.
It is lost as heat from respiration and in waste.
items.e: About 90% is used or lost each step.

items.q: The oak leaves capture 10000 kJ of energy. Using the 10% rule, about how much reaches the caterpillars?
items.e: Divide by 10 for each step: 1 step.

items.q: Food chain: phytoplankton → zooplankton → small fish → tuna. What trophic level are the zooplankton?
items.e: Count from the producer.

items.q: Why are there few foxes compared with oak leaves?
c: Little energy reaches the top of the pyramid.
items.e: Less energy supports fewer animals.

items.q: Which process moves carbon from the geosphere into the atmosphere?
c: formation of fossil fuels over millions of years
items.e: Volcanic eruptions.

items.q: Which process moves carbon from the atmosphere into living things?
items.e: Photosynthesis.

items.q: What happens to the carbon in a dead tree?
c: It stays in the log forever.
Decomposers release it as CO<sub>2</sub>, which plants can use again.
items.e: Matter cycles; energy flows one way.

items.q: Trace a carbon atom. Plankton remains are buried and pressed for millions of years. What forms?
items.e: Each step moves carbon to a new reservoir.

items.q: Trace a carbon atom. Carbon from the air dissolves into the ocean. Which process?
items.e: Each step moves carbon to a new reservoir.

items.q: In a swamp with little oxygen, how do some bacteria break down matter?
c: they cannot break it down at all
anaerobic respiration, which can release methane
items.e: Matter cycles; energy flows one way.

items.q: Where does animals eating plants move carbon?
c: from the hydrosphere into the geosphere
from dead organisms into the atmosphere and soil
from the atmosphere into the hydrosphere
items.e: Animals eating plants moves carbon from producers into consumers.

items.q: Hana observes: “A rabbit eats grass.” What does this show about matter in the ecosystem?
c: Carbon from the air becomes part of the plant.
Matter and energy in the grass move into the rabbit.
Decomposers return carbon and nutrients to the air and soil.
Carbon goes back into the air, where plants can take it in.
items.e: Matter cycles among living and nonliving parts of the ecosystem.

items.q: Noah observes: “A leaf falls and decomposers break it down.” What does this show about matter in the ecosystem?
c: Nitrogen cycles from the soil into plants.
Carbon from the air becomes part of the plant.
Decomposers return carbon and nutrients to the air and soil.
Nutrients return to the soil for plants to use again.
items.e: Matter cycles among living and nonliving parts of the ecosystem.

items.q: Is energy recycled in an ecosystem?
c: No. Energy flows through and leaves as heat; matter is recycled.
items.e: Matter cycles; energy flows one way.

items.q: Which process moves carbon from living things into the atmosphere?
items.e: Respiration.

items.q: Which process moves carbon from the atmosphere into the hydrosphere?
items.e: Ocean absorbing CO<sub>2</sub>.

items.q: Maya observes: “Bacteria in soil change nitrogen into a form plants can use.” What does this show about matter in the ecosystem?
c: Decomposers return carbon and nutrients to the air and soil.
Carbon from the air becomes part of the plant.
Matter and energy in the grass move into the rabbit.
Nitrogen cycles from the soil into plants.
items.e: Matter cycles among living and nonliving parts of the ecosystem.

items.q: Nathan observes: “A dead tree rots on the forest floor.” What does this show about matter in the ecosystem?
c: Nutrients return to the soil for plants to use again.
Carbon from the air becomes part of the plant.
Carbon goes back into the air, where plants can take it in.
Decomposers return carbon and nutrients to the air and soil.
items.e: Matter cycles among living and nonliving parts of the ecosystem.

items.q: Where does volcanic eruptions move carbon?
c: from living things into the atmosphere
from the geosphere into the atmosphere
from the atmosphere into the hydrosphere
from dead organisms into the geosphere
items.e: Volcanic eruptions moves carbon from the geosphere into the atmosphere.

items.q: Trace a carbon atom. A carbon atom in CO<sub>2</sub> enters a grass leaf. Which process?
items.e: Each step moves carbon to a new reservoir.

items.q: Trace a carbon atom. Carbon in coal returns to the air at a power plant. Which process?
items.e: Each step moves carbon to a new reservoir.

items.q: Which process moves carbon from dead organisms into the atmosphere and soil?
items.e: Decomposition.

items.q: Where does ocean absorbing CO<sub>2</sub> move carbon?
c: from the atmosphere into the hydrosphere
from living things into the atmosphere
from the atmosphere into living things
from the geosphere into the atmosphere
items.e: Ocean absorbing CO<sub>2</sub> moves carbon from the atmosphere into the hydrosphere.

items.q: Which process puts carbon from the air into living things?
items.e: Matter cycles; energy flows one way.

items.q: Arjun is modelling respiration. Is carbon dioxide an input or an output?
items.e: Glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water + energy.

items.q: Jayden lists the parts of photosynthesis. Is water an input or an output?
items.e: Water comes from the soil through the roots.

items.q: Equation: 6CO<sub>2</sub> + 6H<sub>2</sub>O → C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>12</sub>O<sub>6</sub> + 6O<sub>2</sub>. How many water molecules are used to make 26 glucose molecules?
items.e: 6 H2O per glucose.

items.q: Equation: 6CO<sub>2</sub> + 6H<sub>2</sub>O → C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>12</sub>O<sub>6</sub> + 6O<sub>2</sub>. A leaf makes 29 glucose molecules. How many O<sub>2</sub> molecules are released?
items.e: 6 O2 per glucose.

items.q: Ethan is modelling respiration. Is usable energy for the cell an input or an output?
items.e: Glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water + energy.

items.q: Ethan is modelling respiration. Is water an input or an output?
items.e: Glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water + energy.

items.q: Kai lists the parts of photosynthesis. Is glucose (sugar) an input or an output?
items.e: Glucose (sugar) stores energy and is used as food and building material.

items.q: Leah is modelling respiration. Is glucose (sugar) an input or an output?
items.e: Glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water + energy.

items.q: Sofia's chart has a row that says it “releases oxygen.” Which process is it?
items.e: Photosynthesis stores energy in sugar; respiration releases it.

items.q: Maya asks where carbon dioxide fits in photosynthesis. Which is true?
c: It comes from the sun and is captured by chlorophyll.
It is released into the air through the leaves.
It comes from the air and enters through tiny openings in leaves (stomata).
It comes from the soil through the roots.
items.e: Carbon dioxide comes from the air and enters through tiny openings in leaves (stomata).

items.q: Aiden asks where light energy fits in photosynthesis. Which is true?
c: It stores energy and is used as food and building material.
It comes from the soil through the roots.
It comes from the sun and is captured by chlorophyll.
It comes from the air and enters through tiny openings in leaves (stomata).
items.e: Light energy comes from the sun and is captured by chlorophyll.

items.q: Equation: 6CO<sub>2</sub> + 6H<sub>2</sub>O → C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>12</sub>O<sub>6</sub> + 6O<sub>2</sub>. A plant takes in 120 CO<sub>2</sub> molecules (with enough water and light). How many glucose molecules can it make?

items.q: Sofia's chart has a row that says it “releases energy from sugar.” Which process is it?
items.e: Photosynthesis stores energy in sugar; respiration releases it.

items.q: Zoe asks where water fits in photosynthesis. Which is true?
c: It is released into the air through the leaves.
It comes from the air and enters through tiny openings in leaves (stomata).

items.e: Water comes from the soil through the roots.

items.q: Sofia lists the parts of photosynthesis. Is light energy an input or an output?

rock weathering that uses CO₂ from rainwater
items.e: Match the process to the flow.
